content.explanation: Making and reading visual work: elements and principles of design, media and technique, and critique as a disciplined conversation about what work does. The branch organizes its concepts from first contact toward independent, integrated practice.

name: Elements of Visual Design
description: Line, shape, color, value, texture, and space — the raw vocabulary every visual work is built from.

observation.question: What is a painting made of, before it is a painting?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can name the core elements of elements of visual design and say what each one does

principle.question: Why does elements of visual design work the way it does?
principle.completionEvidence: Student explains the mechanism in their own words, not by reciting the definition

application.completionEvidence: Student transfers the concept to an unseen case with justified choices

integration.completionEvidence: Student links this concept to its prerequisites in one coherent account

creation.question: Design something original using elements of visual design.
creation.completionEvidence: Student produces an original artifact or proposal and defends its constraints

content.explanation: Every visual work decomposes into elements: line directs the eye, shape organizes, color carries mood and temperature, value models light, texture invites touch, space sets relationships. Skill with elements is skill in controlling what a viewer feels first and understands later — the emotional line works through the hand and eye before the word.
examples: Diagonal lines producing urgency in a poster
Warm palette pulling a subject forward
nonExamples: Calling any use of blue 'sad' without composition analysis
Listing elements without describing their effect

name: Principles of Composition
description: Balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, and unity — the principles that arrange elements into works that hold together.

observation.question: Why does one arrangement hold the eye and another let it go?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can name the core elements of principles of composition and say what each one does

principle.completionEvidence: Student explains the mechanism in their own words, not by reciting the definition

integration.completionEvidence: Student links this concept to its prerequisites in one coherent account

creation.completionEvidence: Student produces an original artifact or proposal and defends its constraints

content.explanation: Principles are the verbs to the elements' nouns. Contrast creates emphasis; repetition at intervals creates rhythm; balanced tension creates unity without monotony. Composition is decision-making about attention: what the viewer sees first, second, and what they return to.
examples: Isolating one bright figure in a muted field for emphasis
Symmetry communicating stability in an architectural drawing
nonExamples: Filling space evenly to avoid decisions
Copying a composition without reading its attention flow

name: Media and Technique
description: The material intelligence of art-making: drawing, paint, clay, digital tools — each with its own affordances and constraints.

observation.question: What does the material want to do?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can name the core elements of media and technique and say what each one does

principle.question: Why does media and technique work the way it does?
principle.completionEvidence: Student explains the mechanism in their own words, not by reciting the definition

application.completionEvidence: Student transfers the concept to an unseen case with justified choices

integration.question: How does media and technique connect with what was learned before it?
integration.completionEvidence: Student links this concept to its prerequisites in one coherent account

creation.question: Design something original using media and technique.
creation.completionEvidence: Student produces an original artifact or proposal and defends its constraints

content.explanation: Media are not neutral containers. Watercolor resists opacity; clay insists on mass; vector tools insist on geometry. Technique is a conversation with these affordances — mastery means knowing what a medium does easily, what it resists, and designing within that grain. The somatic line enters here: hands learn materials the way they learn tools.
examples: Letting watercolor bloom instead of fighting it with control
Choosing charcoal for its smudge-ability when the subject is smoke
nonExamples: Using a medium to imitate another's look at double the effort
Blaming the tool for choices the hand made

name: Critique and Interpretation
description: Talking and writing about work: description, analysis, interpretation, judgment — and receiving critique without defensiveness.

observation.question: How do you say what a work does — and hear what others say yours does?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can name the core elements of critique and interpretation and say what each one does

principle.question: Why does critique and interpretation work the way it does?
principle.completionEvidence: Student explains the mechanism in their own words, not by reciting the definition

application.question: Apply critique and interpretation to a new situation: what would you do and why?
application.completionEvidence: Student transfers the concept to an unseen case with justified choices

integration.question: How does critique and interpretation connect with what was learned before it?
integration.completionEvidence: Student links this concept to its prerequisites in one coherent account

creation.question: Design something original using critique and interpretation.
creation.completionEvidence: Student produces an original artifact or proposal and defends its constraints

content.explanation: Critique is a discipline, not an opinion contest. It moves from description (what is literally there) to analysis (how the principles operate) to interpretation (what the work means) to judgment (does it succeed, by what standard). Giving it honestly and receiving it without collapse is its own developmental practice — the golden shadow of the artist lives here.
examples: Separating 'I dislike it' from 'the focal point is unclear'
Revising after critique because the critique was right
nonExamples: Defense that never asks a question
